principles.statement: Anti-oscillation gating is essential for tree matching sort convergence: without it, type-1 swaps create period-2 oscillation that prevents the permutation from being sorted, reducing scores from 100 to 5.
principles.regime: All tree structures tested: random trees (n~300, diameter~20), path graphs (diameter=n-1), and bushy trees (diameter=6, max_degree~124). n up to 1000.
principles.mechanism: Type-1 swaps move one element closer to its target while displacing another. Without oscillation prevention, the displaced element's routing pressure recreates the same swap opportunity next round, causing infinite oscillation. Depth-parity alternating coloring assigns each parent-child edge a color based on the child's depth modulo 2, ensuring adjacent edges have different colors. Gating type-1 swaps by round parity matching edge color prevents any edge from having consecutive type-1 swaps, breaking the period-2 oscillation cycle. Measured: h-main (with gating) scores 100 vs h-control-negative (without gating) scores 5.
principles.applicability_bounds: Applies to any tree structure. The anti-oscillation mechanism is necessary regardless of tree shape.

principles.statement: Tree DP max-weight matching (O(n) per round) combined with next-step routing weights (type-2=2, type-1=1, type-0=0) achieves optimal or near-optimal sorting on trees, scoring 100/100 averaged across 20 diverse test cases when implemented with cache-efficient data structures.
principles.regime: Trees with n up to 1000, including paths, random trees, and bushy trees. Round budget of 6n. 1-second time limit per test case.
principles.mechanism: The tree DP (dp0[u] = best without matching u to parent, dp1[u] = best with) computes optimal matching in O(n) by exploiting the tree's acyclic structure. Edge weights encode routing benefit: type-2 (both endpoints advance) gets priority weight 2; type-1 (one advances) gets weight 1 when allowed by anti-oscillation. This maximizes per-round progress toward the sorted permutation.
principles.applicability_bounds: The approach is general for any tree. Performance depends on implementation efficiency: the same algorithm scored 89-95 with vector/recursive implementation and 100 with array/iterative implementation.

principles.statement: Implementation efficiency (cache-friendly data structures, iterative algorithms) is critical for competitive programming scoring: the same tree DP algorithm scored 89-95 with std::vector/recursive DP and 100 with array-based/iterative DP due to timing sensitivity.
principles.regime: Competitive programming problems with tight time limits (1 second) and large inputs (n=1000, sum n^2 up to 10^6).
principles.mechanism: Using short (2 bytes) instead of int (4 bytes) for the O(n^2) distance matrix halves memory footprint (~2MB vs ~4MB), improving cache hit rates during BFS. Array-based adjacency lists avoid pointer indirection overhead of std::vector<pair>. Iterative DP via reversed BFS order eliminates function call overhead. Output buffering (fwrite of accumulated buffer) avoids per-character printf overhead.
principles.applicability_bounds: Specific to systems with tight time limits where constant-factor optimizations affect correctness (timeout vs completion). Less relevant for problems with generous time limits.

principles.statement: DFS-timestamp subtree membership queries are a strict replacement for all-pairs BFS distance comparisons in tree matching sort: they produce identical routing decisions (and identical round counts) while reducing precomputation from O(n²) to O(n) and eliminating the ~2MB distance matrix. The DFS approach scored 100 on 3/3 runs vs BFS 100 on 4/5 runs (iter-1), suggesting slightly better timing robustness.
principles.regime: All tree structures tested: random trees (n~303), path graphs (n~493), bushy trees (n~492, max_degree~124). n up to 1000.
principles.mechanism: On a tree rooted at vertex r, for edge (u,v) where v is u's child, element a at u wants to cross to v iff a's target (vertex a) is in v's subtree. The check D[v][a] == D[u][a] - 1 is equivalent to tin[v] <= tin[a] <= tout[v] where tin/tout are DFS timestamps. This O(1) subtree membership test requires only O(n) DFS precomputation vs O(n²) all-pairs BFS, and uses O(2n) int storage vs O(n²) short storage for the distance matrix.
principles.applicability_bounds: Applies specifically to tree graphs where distances between any two vertices can be decomposed into subtree membership. Would not apply to general graphs where shortest paths don't follow a single rooted-tree structure.

principles.statement: Array-based data structures are critical for competitive programming performance through two coupled effects: (1) contiguous-memory children storage eliminates cache misses in the per-round tree DP inner loop, and (2) array types are compatible with #pragma GCC target("avx2") which vector types are not (compilation error in GCC 13). Without array adjacency, DFS+vector scored mean 96.03 (94.37, 94.37, 99.37) vs DFS+array at 100 (3/3). The degradation is larger than the 0.63% expected from cache effects alone because the avx2 incompatibility compounds the penalty.
principles.regime: Competitive programming problems with 1-second time limits, n <= 1000, ~2000 rounds × n nodes per test case. GCC 13+ where avx2 pragma + vector allocator triggers always_inline target mismatch.
principles.mechanism: The tree DP iterates over children of each node ~2000n times total. With ch_arr[u][ci], children are contiguous; with vector<int>, each ch[u] is heap-allocated and non-contiguous. Additionally, #pragma GCC target("avx2") enables AVX2 SIMD instructions which benefit the inner loops, but std::vector's allocator destructor fails to inline when the avx2 target is set (GCC 13 error: always_inline target mismatch). The array version gets both cache efficiency AND avx2 vectorization; the vector version gets neither.
principles.applicability_bounds: Specific to tight time limits where constant-factor and compiler optimizations matter. The avx2 incompatibility is compiler-version-dependent and may change in future GCC versions.

principles.statement: Depth-parity edge coloring is the optimal 2-coloring scheme for anti-oscillation in tree matching sort: alternative coloring schemes (edge-index modulo 2) cause catastrophic convergence failure on bushy trees (6.0n rounds = hitting limit vs 2.0n with depth-parity).
principles.regime: Trees with high-degree vertices (max_degree > 100, diameter ~6). Tested on n~492 bushy trees.
principles.mechanism: Depth-parity coloring assigns each edge color = depth(child) % 2, which is the unique proper 2-coloring of the tree's edge set when viewed as a bipartite graph. This ensures adjacent parent-child edges always have different colors, creating a coherent wave pattern. Edge-index coloring (idx%2) breaks this coherence — adjacent edges may share a color, creating dead rounds where a path has no active edges.
principles.applicability_bounds: Applies to any tree structure. For path graphs, the difference is negligible. For bushy trees with high-degree vertices, depth-parity is strictly required.

principles.statement: Tree DP max-weight matching (not greedy matching) is the necessary matching strategy for achieving score 100 on bushy trees: greedy matching uses 3.88n rounds on bushy trees (max_degree ~124) vs DP's 2.02n, exceeding the 3n scoring threshold and causing consistent score degradation to 99.37.
principles.regime: Bushy trees with max_degree > ~50, where multiple type-2 edges compete for the same internal node
principles.mechanism: At high-degree internal tree nodes, multiple type-2 edges (weight=2) compete for the same parent vertex. The tree DP (O(n) bottom-up computation) considers dp0[u] (leave u unmatched for parent) vs dp1[u] (match u with best child), globally optimizing matching weight. Greedy matching scans edges in input order (idx 1 to n-1), often matching a suboptimal edge early and blocking better alternatives at the same node. On bushy trees (test 20, n≈492, max_degree≈124), this produces 92% more rounds (3.88n vs 2.02n), pushing past the 3n scoring threshold. On low-degree trees (paths, random trees), greedy performs comparably or slightly better than DP because conflicts are rare.
principles.applicability_bounds: Applies specifically to bushy tree structures with high-degree internal nodes (degree > ~10). On path graphs and random trees with low max-degree, greedy matching achieves comparable round counts to DP and the score difference vanishes.

principles.statement: The four critical algorithmic components for score 100 are: (1) anti-oscillation via depth-parity coloring (RP-1, without: 5), (2) tree DP max-weight matching (RP-6, without: 99.37), (3) array-based adjacency (RP-3-refined, without: 96), (4) DFS timestamp routing (RP-4, equivalent to BFS but more timing-robust). Removing any of components 1-3 causes measurable score degradation; the severity decreases by component: 95pts, 0.63pts, 4pts respectively.
principles.regime: Tree matching sort on n≤1000 with 1-second time limit and scoring formula s=(10n-m)/(7n)
principles.mechanism: Three-iteration ablation study systematically removed each component: iter-1 removed anti-oscillation (score 100→5, period-2 oscillation prevents convergence), iter-2 removed array adjacency (score 100→96, cache misses in per-round DP loop cause TLE), iter-3 removed tree DP matching (score 100→99.37, greedy exceeds 3n rounds on bushy trees). DFS timestamps (iter-2) are equivalent to BFS in correctness but use O(n) vs O(n²) precomputation, providing timing headroom.
principles.applicability_bounds: This hierarchy is specific to the scoring formula (10n base, 3n best) and n≤1000 test sizes. For larger n or tighter time limits, the relative importance of components may shift.
